name: poltergeist-class
intent: Records what a Poltergeist costs: a short-lived, typically stateless class created only to run some setup or to invoke a method on some other object, which then vanishes — and the price is an extra concept the reader must hold, for zero encapsulation and zero reuse.
problem: A helper class appears with no state, performs one or two operations that all act on some other object's data or collaborators, and disappears. It was created to anticipate a more complex architecture that never materialised, or because the programmer needed a place to hang a method that has no natural home yet.
context: The definition is Michael Akroyd's, given at Object World West in 1996: as a gypsy wagon or a poltergeist appears and disappears mysteriously, so does this short-lived object, and as a consequence the code is more difficult to maintain and there is unnecessary resource waste; the typical cause is poor object design. The AntiPatterns catalogue places it under proliferation of classes and spurious classes and associations — transient associations, classes with few responsibilities, stateless short-lifecycle classes. The origin story matters for diagnosis: poltergeists are often created because the programmer anticipated a more complex architecture, for example when the same method acts as both client and invoker in a command pattern and the programmer anticipated separating the two phases, and that architecture never arrives. The distinction from legitimate patterns is explicit — a poltergeist is not to be confused with the long-lived, state-bearing objects of MVC, or with tier-separating patterns such as Business Delegate, and a command is generic, reusable and state-bearing while a poltergeist is special-purpose, exists to rattle some chairs, and is rarely used to share state after construction.
benefits: The mistake costs only indirection: the class adds a name, a file and a construction site, and returns no value of its own.
The remedy is deletion, which is the cheapest refactoring in the catalogue: delete the class and inline its functionality into the invoked class, by inheritance or as a mixin.
It is a symptom with a known cause — poor object design — so its appearance is a signal to look at where the missing responsibility actually belongs.
It is unambiguous in practice: a class whose instances are constructed, used once and dropped, with no state carried between uses, is easy to recognise once you look.
tradeoffs: An intermediate helper class is sometimes the right move while a better abstraction is being worked out, and deleting it too early leaves copy-pasted code with nowhere to live — the practitioner discussion is explicit that this is better than duplicating code when there is no better place yet.

'Stateless and short-lived' is a poor criterion on its own. The better questions are whether there is a more natural home for the method (the view's own class, an extension method on the right type, a static on an existing class), whether more than one caller uses it, and whether it needs state — a builder with configuration is a perfectly valid abstraction.
Removing a poltergeist that was written in anticipation of an architecture can be thrown away again: the architecture may arrive, and the helper may then become legitimate.

The cost is smaller than it looks. A two-line helper does not slow anyone measurably down; the real harm is proportional to how many of them there are and how confidently the names imply a structure that does not exist.

Inheritance is the suggested deletion mechanism (inline into the invoked class, possibly by inheritance or as a mixin) but it can harden the design at exactly the wrong moment if the invoked class is not otherwise subclassed.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the codebase while the smell is present. The runtime axes barely move — a poltergeist is a construction and two virtual calls, so performance, reliability and security are essentially unaffected, which is why it survives for years. The axes that suffer are discoverability (the class name advertises a responsibility that lives elsewhere) and maintainability: a proliferation of them is precisely the mechanism the AntiPatterns catalogue lists. Maintainability sits mid rather than low because the damage is proportional to the count, not to any single instance.

participants.responsibility: The short-lived, typically stateless object: constructed, used to perform initialisation or to invoke methods on another class, and discarded.
participants.notes: It adds no functionality and no encapsulation — the Wikipedia example is a UserCreator constructed only to call UserManager.createUser.

participants.responsibility: The real class that holds the state and the behaviour the poltergeist reaches; its method is the one that should exist.
participants.notes: The fix is to move the call there and delete the helper.

participants.responsibility: The design that was imagined but never built, and the reason the helper was written in the first place.
participants.notes: Typical: separating the client and invoker roles of a command pattern before the pattern was needed.

use_cases: A `UserCreator` class whose constructor takes a name, constructs a `UserManager` and calls `createUser` — the canonical example, with the fix being to construct the manager and call the method directly.
A `DialogHelper` holding one method that adds a welcome dialog to a view, when the view's own class is the obvious home.
A builder object that configures nothing and exists only to wrap one call in a fluent chain of one step.
A `ServiceInitializer` constructed, used to call one setter, and dropped, in every place a service is set up.
A class created because the programmer anticipated splitting a command's client and invoker roles, before there was a second client to separate them from.
avoid_when: The helper carries real configuration or state and is used more than once — a builder with parameters is a valid abstraction, not a poltergeist.

It is the deliberate intermediate step toward an abstraction nobody has designed yet, which the practitioner discussion argues is better than duplicating code in the meantime; give it an expiry instead of deleting it.
The language cannot attach the behaviour to the right type (a sealed third-party class), in which case an extension method or a module-level function is the local idiom and not a smell.
It is a genuine value object, builder or strategy — stateless in the field sense but with a clear identity, contract and lifecycle that is not 'constructed, called, dropped'.
It exists purely for testability as a seam for a static or hard-to-construct collaborator; that is a real reason, and it should be named in the class comment.
The class is a command or a delegate that carries state and is queued, retried or reused — the AntiPatterns text is explicit that poltergeists are not these.
pitfalls: Judging on 'stateless and short-lived' alone, which the practitioner discussion shows catches perfectly good helpers: the real tests are whether a more natural home exists, whether more than one caller uses it, and whether it needs state.
Moving the method to the nearest plausible class instead of the right one, which relocates the envy's knowledge rather than removing it.
Rescuing the helper by giving it more methods, converting a poltergeist into a utility class — a worse smell with the same name on the diagram.
Keeping it because 'the architecture will need it', which is how speculative helpers multiply; they are only worth keeping with a named trigger.
Using the name `*Helper`, `*Utils` or `*Manager` in the rescue, which makes the absence of a responsibility look like a design decision on the class diagram.

related_patterns_notes.command: Command is the closest relative and the clearest contrast: a command is generic, carries enough state to be reused, and is often queued or deferred. A poltergeist is special-purpose, does one thing to another object, and disappears.
related_patterns_notes.business-delegate: The AntiPatterns text explicitly rules business delegate out of this category: it is a long-lived, state-bearing, tier-separating object, which is the opposite of a stateless short-lived helper.
related_patterns_notes.method-object: Method Object is the sanctioned version of what a poltergeist usually wants to be: a named object for one complex algorithm that carries the algorithm's parameters as state, instead of a stateless wrapper around somebody else's method.
related_patterns_notes.builder: A builder that accumulates configuration across several calls is a real abstraction; the poltergeist is the degenerate one-step builder with nothing to configure.
related_patterns_notes.service-activator: Service activator is a role in a distributed architecture, and a poltergeist that exists only to activate a service is the version of it that has no service boundary behind it.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy is a poltergeist's opposite: a strategy holds no state about its collaborators but is a first-class, swappable, named algorithm rather than a one-call wrapper.

anti_patterns: The constructor that does the work: a class whose constructor initialises another object and whose only method is then called once, after which it is discarded.
The `*Helper` / `*Utils` rescue of a single method whose natural home is the class that owns the data it operates on.
A one-step fluent builder that configures nothing and returns the thing it was given.
The speculative helper written ahead of an architecture, never reused, and named as if the architecture existed.
A poltergeist chain: three transient objects that call each other once, where one call would have done.
A helper that exists only to satisfy an imagined interface point, so an empty class and an interface method exist with no implementation behind them.
Rescuing a poltergeist by accumulating unrelated one-line methods into it, turning a transient class into a utility class.
design_principles: Objects exist for a reason: a class that carries no state and no invariant of its own should be a function, and a name that implies a responsibility should point at the code that has it.
If it does not need to exist twice, it should not be a class: lifetime, identity and construction only earn their cost when an object outlives its creation site.
Least knowledge and least indirection: the extra concept in a poltergeist costs the reader a name to hold and buys no encapsulation.

Anticipate with a seam, not with a class: when you expect a future architecture, extract an interface at the boundary and let the implementation change, instead of writing the speculative structure now.
Encapsulate or vanish: a class that adds no encapsulation should be deleted rather than preserved for symmetry with the diagram.
best_practices: Look for the lifetime, not the name: construction immediately followed by one or two calls with no reference retained is the signal, and it is greppable (`new X(...)` with no assignment to a variable of that type).

Ask the three questions from the practitioner discussion before deleting: is there a more natural home (the view's own class, an extension on the right type, a static on an existing class)? Is it used by more than one caller? Does it need state?
Prefer deletion to inheritance as the remedy — move the call into the invoked class and delete the helper — since inheritance cements a design that was never validated.

Replace with the local idiom where a home does not exist: an extension method on the sealed third-party type (C#, Kotlin, Swift), a package-level function (Go, Rust, Python), or a module/class-function (Scala).
If it is a genuine intermediate step toward an abstraction, keep it with a named trigger and a date, so it is a plan rather than an anchor.
Name honestly during review: a class called `PaymentHelper` is a smell signal; `InvoiceCollector` is a class someone can find the responsibility in.
Add a lint rule or review question for the constructor-does-the-work shape, since it is easy to check and reliably wrong.
sources: Michael Akroyd, definition given at Object World West, 1996, quoted in Wikipedia's Poltergeist article: 'As a gypsy wagon or a poltergeist appears and disappears mysteriously, so does this short lived object. As a consequence the code is more difficult to maintain and there is unnecessary resource waste. The typical cause for this anti-pattern is poor object design.'

AntiPatterns (Bell Labs) Development AntiPattern briefing — poltergeists listed under proliferation of classes and spurious classes and associations: transient associations, classes with few responsibilities, stateless short-lifecycle classes.

Practitioner discussion distinguishing poltergeists from commands ('generic, can be reusable and represent a configurable action') and from functors, and arguing that 'stateless and short-lived' alone is not a useful criterion — the questions that matter are whether a more natural home exists, whether more than one caller uses it, and whether it needs state.
Robert C. Martin, 'The Poltergeist Pattern' / Riel's object-oriented anti-pattern taxonomy as cited by the AntiPatterns briefing (Riel 1996).
